To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
nitrogen fixation in the roots of a conifer, Lepidothamnu s fonkii, is carried out in nodules by diazotroph Beijerinckiacea e.

(i) root nodules of L. fonki are inhabited by active diazotrophic members of the Beijerinckiaceaea and (ii) BNF in nodulated roots, rhizosphere and intact plants of L.fonkii is high and may contribute significantly to N nutrition of the plants.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of a new type of root nodule, the first report on associative BNF in a gymnosperm, and the first report on BNF in a conifer.
the discovery of associative BNF by a conifer in the Podocarpacea family and the identification of the diazotroph as a member of the Beijerinckiacea.
the discovery and characterization of the first known root nodules in the Podocarpacea and with associative BNF in a conifer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the nodules of L. fonki are not a symbiotic association but rather an associative association with Beijerinckiacea.
BNF by Beijerinckiacea in nodules of L. fonki is a novel pathway of N acquisition in ombrotrophy peatlands.
the root nodules of L. fonki are not true root nodules, but rather represent an exclusive habitat for a specific Beijerinckiacean symbiont.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the conifer L. fonkiii recruits diazotrophic members of the family Beijerinckiacea from the surrounding peat to form root nodules, which in turn provide a unique habitat for these bacteria.
BNF is an important pathway for the nitrogen nutrition of L. fonki in ombrotropic peatlands.
L. fonkiii is a pioneer in nitrogen fixing nodules in the plant kingdom.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BNF is a widespread phenomenon in the rhizophsere of conifers, but the role of BNF in N acquisition has been underestimated.
